subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, April 29, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Acting' Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Woodsworth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) announced to the country that his government had reduced the national debt for the year ending March 31, 1924, by the sum of $30,400,000 odd. The member for St. Law-renee-St. George (Mr. Marler), speaking yesterday, estimated that the Acting Minister of Finance should have shown a deficit of about $2,000,000, and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), who followed him, stated that he agreed with the member for St. Lawrence-St. George and that he also believed that the minister should have shown a deficit.
By a simple mathematical calculation based on the principle enunciated by the member for St. Lawrence-St. George and by the member for Brome-principles which, I may say, I personally believe in, and principles upon which all past ministers of finance have acted-I estimate that the Minister of Finance this year should have shown a deficit of $26,906,850.43 instead of a surplus of $30,400,000 odd.	'
I would like to examine for a few minutes the statement furnished to the House by the Acting Minister of Finance. He stated that last year the national debt had increased by $31,641,067.01. If this be true, there must have been an improvement this year over last year of $62,000,000. Now, what are the facts? The returns of the Finance department show that this year's total revenues were larger than last year's by $2,383,000 odd. In addition to that, there was some found money, admitted by the minister to be such, of $9,622,000 odd. Similarly last year they had found money amounting to nearly $8,-
200,000.	They were therefore more fortunate this year than last by nearly a million and
a half dollars, showing a total improvement of about $3,800,000.
There are four classes of expenditure, ordinary, capital, special, and National Railways. Our capital expenditure increased last year by roughly, $3,500,000. Our ordinary expenditure diminished by $1,000,000 and our special expenditure diminished by $107,000, leaving a net increase in these three classes of expenditure of nearly $2,500,000. If we deduct the total increase of expenditure outside of National Railways from the total increase of revenue, we see that the showing for the year 1923-24 is better than the showing for 1922-23 by $1,385,000. If bur ordinary expenditure has only improved by the small amount that I have indicated, how does the minister find his betterment of $62,000,000? Obviously he has issued bonds, one issue for $50,000,000 on the railways, another issue for $22,500,000 on railway equipment, making $72,500,000 in all, but he has not charged that, as has always been done in the past, to the national debt. So that if you deduct the minister's supposed surplus of $30,500,000 ,t shows an actual deficit of $42,090,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Would the hon member
permit a question? This is merely to clear up what I think is a misconception. In figuring the surplus or deficit, does the hon. member take into account any moneys expended by way of betterment to the railways, what yon might call capital expenditure?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I will come to that. What
I was going to say was this. The minister has announced that of the $50,000,000 bond issue, he has cash in hand of $15,184,000, so that you may in all fairness, though the minister did not say anything about it in his budget speech, deduct that from what would appear to be the total deficit of $42,090,000, whereupon you arrive at the figure I gave of $26,906,850.43 as the actual deficit.
The hon. member for Brome stated, and I entirely agree with him, that the obligations of the National Railways are direct obligations in the same way that the Intercolonial railway obligations were direct, and that they should therefore be added to our national debt. With regard to betterments referred to by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Euler), the hon. member for Brome suggested that the national debt should be decreased by an amount equivalent to the extent to which the position of the National Railways had been improved by the value of the betterment. With that I do not agree; that would be an entirely wrong principle to adopt. If you value the betterments on the National Rail-
The Budget-Mr. Clark

ways and deduct the amount of that value from the total amount paid to the railways, you will have to do the same thing on all public works, on all canals and every other capital expenditure undertaken by the government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: May I interject something there? Is there not a difference to be drawn between an ordinary public work such as a wharf or a canal which is not productive of any revenue, and a railway, which, properly managed should carry itself?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I do not admit that our
canals do not produce a revenue, nor do I admit that we have not other public works that produce a revenue. But in any case the fact is that up until the end of 1923 this country had paid over $580,000,000 more on National Railways than the country considered National Railways were worth to us. Now let us go back to the year 1920, when a new system was adopted by the then Minister of Finance of writing off and adding to the national debt every non-active security. He states in his budget address of May 18, 1920:
It is obvious that the advances to the Canadian Northern, Grand Trunk Pacific and Grand Trunk Railway Companies cannot be treated as active assets. They are not at the moment realizable;' further, no interest is being paid, and in some cases the principal as well as interest is overdue. As is well known, Canada is now the owner of the Canadian Northern, receiver for the Grand Trunk Pacific, and steps have been taken for the acquisition of the Grand Trunk. While the railways have potential value, at the present time the fact is that the country itself owns the Canadian Northern and is responsible for the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific, with resultant heavy cost to the taxpayer.
Assets which are not readily convertible, as the specie reserve is, or are not interest producing, are not such assets as ought to be deducted from the gross debt. They are inactive, they are items of such a character as might well be placed in a suspense account. At any rate, whatever may be their future value, however great it may be, they are not assets of such a character as to directly reduce the gross debt any more than the other capital accounts of the country ought to be deducted from it.
In that year, 1920, the Minister of Finance wrote off securities and advances to the value of $272,000,000 odd, and added that amount to the national debt. In 1921 he added another $100,000,000 approximately, and in 1922 the Minister of Finance in the present government (Mr. Fielding) added approximately another $100,000,000, and last year another $70,000,000, making a total of $558,000,000 odd of non-active securities that were written off, indicating that the railways had cost us that much more than they were worth to the country. This year we have it suggested that similar securities that have been considered of no value in the past should now be considered

as specie securities readily realizable. I submit that that has been done for the purpose of showing a balanced budget and a surplus, with the result that the country has been deceived, and the comparison between this year and last that has been given to this House and to the country is on a basis which is entirely unfair. The result of that system is going to mean that in the future the national debt cannot be ascertained with any degree of certainty, and Canada's credit will suffer accordingly, because investors will never be able to ascertain what the margin of security on this country's assets may be.
To show further how absolutely inaccurate the minister's figures are, he states in his budget speech that the railways have cost us $23,781,664, whereas the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) in a return stated that the total deficit for the calendar year of 1923 was $44,-
962,000.	What I would like to know is how this enormous deficit was reduced to $23,000,000 between January 1, 1924, and March 31, 1924, or was it reduced at all, and where did the minister get the money, unless as I stated he got it from the bond issues, and he has used that money for the purpose of paying ordinary deficits on the National railways?
Now I come to a different branch of this budget debate, and it is necessary before going into the general conditions of this country first of all to consider briefly agricultural conditions in Canada. At the outset I am prepared to admit that farming conditions are not satisfactory, and that we must find remedies for the existing conditions. At the same time I want to ask, are farming conditions in any country in a satisfactory condition? Are they in a satisfactory condition in the United States? Are they in a satisfactory condition in free trade England? Undoubtedly farming in free trade England is dead'. In the United States farming conditions resemble ours, but our conditions are better because we have cheaper land and because our prairie lands will still grow wheat, whereas in the competing sections of the United States immediately to the south, in the Dakotas, the land will no longer raise good crops. To use an expression which some of my Progressive friends have used, the land in the Dakotas is mined out.
I would like to refer to the presidential address of Mr. Coolidge before congress this year. He stated:
The distress is most acute among those wholly dependent on one crop. The wheat crop was greatly expanded and has not yet been sufficiently reduced.
A large amount is raised for export which has to meet competition in the world's market of large

The Budget-Mr. Clark
amounts raised on lands much cheaper and much more productive. He (the farmer) must be assisted by reorganization of the freight rate structure, which will reduce charges on his production. The acreage of wheat is too large. Unless we can meet the world market at a profit we must stop raising for export.
Now that is quite a different policy from that advocated by the wheat growers of this country. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) advocates that the way to cure the position of the wheat grower in Canada is to abolish protection; sound the death knell of protection, and that will cure all ills. I might refer for just a moment to his argument. He says, "I trust that it will be the death knell of protection." He refers to the depressed conditions that existed at the time the Laurier government came into power in 1896, and he attributes those conditions practically, exclusively to the high tariff. And then he boasts that the best condition Canada ever had existed between 1896 and 1911. But he admits that the tariff structure was not much changed. This is what he said:
In 1896 we had a change of government: Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into office. Now no one is going to suggest that over night Sir Wilfrid Laurier changed the whole fiscal policy of this country. He did not. But he did one thing-he succeeded in removing the quarantine regulations against cattle.
A great argument for free trade! Now, what I say is this, that at no time since the National Policy came into effect has any government of Canada pronounced a policy of free trade until that policy was announced by the Minister of the Interior in his recent speech. And I say that such a policy will act as a boomerang on those reponsible for it. Furthermore-and to my mind this is the most serious feature of the matter-it will not tend to promote a better feeling between the West and the East. In the past there has unfortunately existed a feeling in the West against the East. That will now be changed I fear to a bitter feeling on the part of the industrial interests of this country towards the section of Canada that is insisting now upon a policy of free trade. You cannot promote the interests of any one great industry by killing another great industry. In addition to that, such a policy will destroy what is more vital to the wheat grower-more particularly to the farmers of Ontario, Quebec, and the provinces other than the prairie provinces-namely, their home market. And even to the prairie farmer, despite the statement of the Minister of the Interior, the home market is absolutely vital. The home market is vital to every interest in this country-whether it be mixed farming, or fruit growing, or manufacturing, or any other walk of life. .
I should like now to give a few figures showing what this home market meant to the agriculturists in the year ending August 31, 1923. We will take grains first. The proportion of barley exported was 19.4 per cent. The proportion of beans exported was 7.1 per cent. The proportion of buckwheat exported was 6.3 per cent. The proportion of corn exported was 2 per cent. The proportion of oats was 4.7 per cent. I may point out that the value of the oat crop was over 50 per cent that of the wheat crop of the same year, which means that over 95 per cent of the oat crop of this country was consumed in the home market.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Who provided that 95 per cent of the home market for oats and other coarse grains?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I have not the figures. However, I have no doubt at all that the market was provided by all interests; by the wholesalers in the city who use horses; by the lumber men who use horses in the woods, and by the farmers themselves. I am not detracting from the fact that you sell some oats to farmers or that you use some oats yourselves: That is quite true. But how many bushels of oats do you suppose were eaten by the good Scotch Presbyterians in the form of oatmeal? I imagine it would amount to a good quantity. To continue with my figures. The proportion of peas exported was 7.8 per cent and the proportion of rye exported 31.4 per cent. Of wheat the proportion exported was 57.4 per cent.
I think it was the hon. member for Battle-ford (Mr. McConica) who some time ago asked the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) what difference there w,as between selling our produce to ten millions of foreigners and to ten million residents of Canada. With respect to that I ask: Is it of no value to increase the population of Canada? Do we want to increase the population of this Dominion, or do we want Canadians to continue their present exodus to the United States-a course that the present government is permitting? I question very much if there is a dairy farmer, or a producer of eggs, or a producer of beef or mutton in Canada who would suggest for one moment that the home market is not more vital to him than any other market that could be provided.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
When we
have an exportable surplus of eggs, and of d,airy and meat products, would not my hon. friend say that the price received for those products determines the price in the home market?
The Budget-Mr. Clark

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: That does not for one moment detract from the value of the home market. My hon. friend must remember I am talking of the value of the home market.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

In principle that may be true as to wheat. But I think that the wheat growers of Canada to-day are receiving about the same price for their wheat that they received in 1913. Now I suggest that that price would be larger if we in-
4 p.m. creased the home market by an infinitely greater degree. This year we have 180,000 less consumers of wheat in Canada than we had last year; that number of our best Canadians has been driven across the borders of the United States. Is that market of any value to the wheat growers of this country?

I have already quoted the president of the United States on that point, and he says that their exportable surplus is too large and that they must decrease the acreage. He will welcome, I am sure, these 180,000 wheat-eating Canadians to eat up that surplus. It has been disputed in this House; it was disputed by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George that Canada is losing its citizens at the rate that has been suggested. Has the

speechtext:
I have not those figures,
but hon. members might note this, that the tremendous percentage of people who have left have come from that portion of Canada Which 'lies east of Fort William.
I should like to deal for a few minutes with the effect which the present policy of the government has upon the industries of this country. I have made a computation, and I find that ten tariff items of the present tariff amendments vitally affect 917 industries in Canada. There are only 37 tariff changes out of a thousand or more items. Let me refer to some specific industries and the effect upon them.
For the purpose of illustrating the effect of the reductions on logging machinery I will take some industry in my province, British Columbia. For the purpose of illustrating the effect on the mining industry, I will take an industry in Quebec. I find that in my city numerous manufacturers of logging machinery are vitally affected by this tariff. Until the war was nearly over, those manufacturers had made very little equipment for the logging industry; but they built up their plants during the war for

The Budget-Mr. Clark
munitions and other purposes, and as soon as the war closed, they adapted those plants for the purpose of making logging machinery. Under the protective system, in the particular lines of industry which they manufacture, we find that last year they controlled approximately 80 per cent of the market for logging machinery in British Columbia. By the way, I do not think this government or anybody else can for one moment accuse British Columbia of having old established manufacturing industries, industries which should have established themselves, got on their feet and be past the stage when protection should be required. I think it will be admitted quite freely by everybody that these are still infant industries. I might also mention this fact, that the logging industry in British Columbia is competing with the logging industry in the states of Oregon and Washington. We find that the logging industry in those two states is making a bitter complaint to the federal government at Washington, asking that something be done to stop our British Columbia logs from flowing in and competing with their logs on the Pacific coast. As a matter of fact,
I would rather welcome action on the part of the United States government to that effect, because if our government will not deal with the situation and will not put an export duty upon our raw materials, such as our logs, that we should manufacture into lumber here, I rather hope the American government will impose a duty and thus force our Canadians to manufacture their logs into lumber at home. Let me read what a few of these manufacturers think of [DOT]the policy of the government as indicated in this budget. It is incidentally significant to me to find that practically the only people who argue against any sort of protection are wheat growers and those who are not engaged in industry in any sense of the word and who therefore know nothing about industrial problems. They advance what I submit are the views of economists, which, elaborated nearly a hundred years ago, are no longer applicable to business conditions in this country, or any other country for that matter. This is what one of these ih-fant industries says:
The cost to the British Columbia logger is considerably less than to the United States logger and it would appear at first glance that we have no need to worry about American competition, but that is very far from being the case. The logging industry is to a very large extent controlled by American capital and the most of the logging superintendents and foremen are American citizens who have obtained their training in the United States. These men are all partial to American made goods and it is only because of the
large difference in the price that we can induce them to try the Canadian product. It is the American influence we have to fight, and reduction of the duty takes away the only weapon we have to fight with.
The hon. member for Brome, last night made the statement that bur people would buy Canadian goods in preference to American goods if we could sell them as cheaply.
I should like, to take the hon. member to British Columbia and let him go through the logging camps and ascertain for himself just what conditions these people have to contend with. I do not know to what extent, but I can say that to a tremendous extent, this industry in British Columbia is controlled by American capital, and many logging superintendents are American men trained in American ways and therefore prefer American machinery. Yet the hon. member for Brome has the hardihood to say that these men would buy Canadian machinery in preference to the American manufacture if they could get it at the same price.

We emphatically piotest against any reduction in the tariff on logging cars. Last year we commenced manufacturing these. They had always been imported previously. We sell these cars for $1,750 Vancouver; the American price is $1,900 and our actual cost of labour and material is $1,442 without allowing anything for overhead and profit. This will spell ruin for our steel industry and it is done in order that some of our manufacturing concerns may be permitted to buy from the United States various component parts entering into their finished product.

ment an industry in my constituency, a large creosoting industr3r in which there is invested nearly $400,000 of capital. This industry makes creosoted piling and creosoted railway ties. I asked that protection should be given to that industry, but that, of course, was refused. I was, however, assured by the Minister of Finance and by his tariff expert that the sales tax would be eliminated from the creosote which entered into that product. I know that the Minister of Finance intended to do that, but the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Bureau) interpreted the act otherwise, and the result was that, instead of the industry being subjected to a sales tax of 2| per cent on every gallon of creosote that went into its product, it was increased to 6 per cent, although the Minister of Finance intended, as he stated to me, that it should be free from the sales tax. It has in stock to-day 380,000 gallons which retails at about 95 cents a gallon and is sold wholesale at about 60 cents a gallon. There we have an outlay of about $200,000. MJr point is this, 50 per cent of the value of that company's product consists of the raw creosote that goes into the timber. Therefore, the effect of the law as it stood prior to the bringing down of this budget, was that on every stick of creosoted timber that came into this country, from the United States, a subsidy of 3 per cent was given to the Americans. In conclusion I want to re-affirm, that the financial statement presented by the Acting Minister of Finance is a gross misrepresentation of the actual financial condition of the country; and that the minister has adopted a new system of accounting. The minister has eliminated expenditures of large amounts actually required to meet railway deficits, hitherto always properly added to the public expenditures and taken into account when computing the national debt. Under this new system we can never accurately determine the national debt, and Canada's credit will consequently suffer because investors in Dominion securities will not be able to determine the margin of security; in fact, they will not know whether the actual indebtedness of the country is greater or less than the total assets. speechtext:
I wish to associate myself with the speakers who have preceded me in expressing my regrets at the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the hope that we may soon again see him in his accustomed seat. The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is to be congratulated upon his first budget; he has achieved this year what has been the ambition of his predecessors, namely, a balanced budget. The budget shows a surplus of revenue over ordinary expenditure of $67,750,000 and it will reduce by $24,000,000 the burden of taxation which has borne so heavily upon the agricultural and labouring classes. The
returns for the eleven months ended February 29 indicate a continued healthy growth of Canadian and foreign trade. Already both imports and exports exceed those of 1923, and the balance of trade favourable to Canada for the eleven months is $158,424,707. The balance of trade is regarded by many persons as the barometer indicating trade conditions and we must accept these figures as indisputable proof of a steady return to stability. We are gradually emerging from conditions created by the enormous expenditures and , losses incurred in the world's war, and in common with all other countries we have had to adapt ourselves to entirely new conditions.
I feel safe in saying that no other country can look forward to the future with more confidence and optimism than can Canada.
Senator Ingalls of the United States said somewhere that out of every great struggle some man or sect or nation has emerged with higher possibilities, greater opportunities, broader liberties, purer religion and a greater capacity for happiness. I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that Canada is now emerging from its participation in the world's war with greater opportunities for the future. Possessing a sturdy and law-abiding population of instinctive common sense, with unlimited natural resources which all the world requires, with water-power and transportation facilities unequalled anywhere, Canada must, if its people will unite in one national effort and every class of our population do its duty and contribute its fair share to the restoration of our losses and the payment of the debt incurred by war, soon return to normalcy. In order to achieve this end, which is the ambition of every true Canadian, it will be necessary to forget that there exists in Canada an East and a West. There is no room here for sectionalism. The welfare of Canada is the concern of all.
One of the most contentious questions we have had to deal with since confederation is the tariff-always a most difficult problem for a nation that has industries to protect, agriculture to encourage and a wage-earning class of consumers demanding a' high standard of living. The adjustment of a tariff in such a way that it will bear equally on all classes of society, without interfering with the progress or stability of industry is, as I have said, a difficult problem. Our tariff has been the rock upon which governments have been most frequently wrecked. Every government has endeavoured to evolve a tariff policy which would be acceptable to all. the various classes that compose our population. And it must be admitted that to the liberal party is due tho
The Budget-Mr. Lapierre

When this has been successfully accomplished, a more economical system of distribution must be found. In Canada to-day we have a highly efficient but very expensive system of distribution. From the time our commodities leave the producer and reach the consumer they pass through the hands of several middlemen, such as wholesalers, jobbers, agents, retailers, and so forth, all of whom tack on from 5 to 50 per cent to the cost of the goods as they pass them along from one to the other and finally to the consumer. There are too many middlemen engaged in distributing commodities. The streets of our cities and towns and villages are lined with stores, shops, emporiums, bazaars, and so forth, many of them engaged in the same line of business, and most of them getting more for the service they render than the wages earned by the producers. The office buildings of our cities are honeycombed with offices of agents and representatives of manufacturing companies, most of them getting more for the services they render than the wages earned by the producers. When you have reduced the cost of distribution and transportation you will have taken the first step towards relieving the wage earner of much of the burden he is asked to bear.
By reducing the tariff on instruments of production such as farming, mining, lumbering and logging machinery, the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has made the first serious move towards fostering our mining and lumbering industries, a movement of momentous importance which will be received with great satisfaction by the mining and lumbering interests, especially in New Ontario and northern Quebec-that vast region possessing potential wealth greater than any other area of its size in the world; a region which is pronounced by eminent geologists as the greatest exposure of mineral wealth known to science; a region that is destined to take a foremost place as a producer of mineral wealth.
The development of our natural resources will help to solve our transportation problems, will give employment to thousands of wage earners, and the great consumption of various commodities, required in the development of these industries will stimulate trade and commerce throughout Canada.
The importance of mineral resources in the economic structure of Canada has been vastly magnified in modern times and these resources are the basis of industrial strength and progress. The pre-Cambrian area of Canada, surrounding Hudson bay, and occupying more than half of the entire surface of the country, is described by Dr. C. V. Corless, the eminent geologist of the Mond Nickel Company, as the greatest single exposure of mother earth's basement in the world, and it is there we are finding her richest treasures stored for future use. The pre-Cambrian formation appears right across northern Ontario. It extends in from the province of Quebec and extends out to Manitoba. The mines in northern Ontario are on the outer edge of the pre-Cambrian formation.

The most remarkable feature of the preCambrian formation in northern Ontario is the variety of metallic and non-metallic ores, found in a comparatively small area within a radius of a few hundred miles. Gold, silver, nickel and copper mines are operating with increasing production, and the country, as yet, has really only been scratched.
There are three distinct camps within this area-the Sudbury district producing nickel, the Porcupine district producing gold, and the Cobalt area producing silver. The mines of the Sudbury district are now producing nickel and copper at the rate of close to twenty-five million dollars a year, and are running neck and neck with the gold mines of Ontario for the position of leading place in the mining industries of this province.
Mining operations of the International Nickel Company are centered at Creighton mine, where work continues to disclose enormous resources of nickel-copper ore, extending far beyond previously known limits. Some of the recently developed ore contains between 30 and 35 per cent metal as compared with a general average of from 5 to 6 per cent. Approximately 75,000 tons of material are being hoisted monthly from the Creighton mine, of which about 60,000 tons go to the smelter. The ore is yielding 5 per cent metal, in the proportion of two of nickel to one of copper. With nickel commanding about 25 cents a pound, and copper having a market value of 14 cents to 15 cents per pound, the company is producing a value of upwards of $1,300,000 per month, or at the rate of $16,000,000 a year.
The Mond Nickel Company is now employing between 800 and 900 men and is handling about 1,000 tons of ore daily, the operation being at the rate of about one-third that of the International Nickel Company.
The company holds about 29,000 acres of mining land and has a 1,500-ton smelter at Coniston, with refining works at Clydach, South Wales. In one section of the property, work has been carried on to a depth of 3,600 feet.
The British North American Company has a smelter capacity of 1,600 tons per day with a refinery located at Deschenes, Quebec. The
combined facilities are sufficient to produce nickel at the rate of 15,000,000 pounds annually. About 1,000 tons per day have been the recent rate of operation. The nickel and copper contents of the area have a ratio of about 55 of copper to 100 of nickel. Ore reserves on the British American are made up of about 16,000,000 tons of ore. These three corporations form the nickel group of our mining industries in the north and produce 85 per cent of the world's production of nickel
